items.stem: What is meant by Newton's first law of motion?
items.answer: The law that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced force
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Newton's first law of motion – the law that an object remains at rest or in uniform motion in a straight line unless acted upon by an unbalanced force.

items.stem: Seat belts are worn in cars to:
items.answer: prevent passengers from being thrown forward when the car stops suddenly
items.markingKey: (c) prevent passengers from being thrown forward when the car stops suddenly.
options: increase the speed of the car
prevent passengers from being thrown forward when the car stops suddenly
balance the forces on the car

items.stem: Why do passengers in a moving bus lean forward when the driver applies brakes suddenly?
items.answer: The lower body stops with the bus, but the upper body tends to continue moving due to inertia of motion.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inertia of motion. 1 mark: explanation.

items.stem: Two forces of 50 N to the right and 25 N to the left act on a wooden block on a table. Are the forces balanced? Find the net force and its effect.
items.answer: Unbalanced; net force 25 N towards the right; the object accelerates in that direction.
items.markingKey: Net force = 50 − 25 = 25 N (1 mark); unbalanced, so it changes the state of motion (1 mark).

items.stem: Explain why a person standing in a moving train falls when the train turns sharply.
items.answer: The body tends to continue moving in a straight line due to inertia while the train turns, so the person is thrown outward.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inertia of direction. 1 mark: thrown outward.

items.stem: Explain using Newton's laws why it is dangerous to jump out of a moving bus.
items.answer: Feet stop on touching the ground, but the body keeps moving forward due to inertia (first law), so the person falls forward; the large change in momentum in a short time gives a large force (second law).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inertia. 1 mark: falls forward. 1 mark: force.

items.stem: Two forces of 20 N to the right and 50 N to the left act on a wooden block on a table. Are the forces balanced? Find the net force and its effect.
items.answer: Unbalanced; net force 30 N towards the left; the object accelerates in that direction.
items.markingKey: Net force = 50 − 20 = 30 N (1 mark); unbalanced, so it changes the state of motion (1 mark).

items.stem:
Assertion (A): An object in uniform motion must have an unbalanced force on it.
Reason (R): Balanced forces do not change the state of motion.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: A is false, but R is true.
items.markingKey: (d) A false: no net force needed for uniform motion; R true.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: Two forces of 40 N to the right and 50 N to the left act on a trolley. Are the forces balanced? Find the net force and its effect.
items.answer: Unbalanced; net force 10 N towards the left; the object accelerates in that direction.
items.markingKey: Net force = 50 − 40 = 10 N (1 mark); unbalanced, so it changes the state of motion (1 mark).

items.stem: When a card on a glass is flicked quickly, the coin on it falls into the glass. Explain.
items.answer: The card moves away quickly, but the coin, due to inertia of rest, stays in place and falls into the glass under gravity.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: inertia of rest. 1 mark: gravity.

items.stem: Which term is described here? "Forces acting on an object whose resultant is zero, so they do not change its state of motion."
items.markingKey: (d) Balanced forces is forces acting on an object whose resultant is zero, so they do not change its state of motion.

A cricket fielder draws his hands back while catching a fast ball to:
items.answer: increase the time of impact and reduce the force
items.markingKey: (a) increase the time of impact and reduce the force.
options: increase the time of impact and reduce the force
reduce the mass of the ball

items.stem:
Assertion (A): A bullet fired from a gun can kill though its mass is small.
Reason (R): Its momentum is large because of its very high velocity.
Choose the correct option.
items.answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
items.markingKey: (a) R explains A.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

items.stem: What force is needed to give a mass of 1500 kg an acceleration of 4 m/s²?
A car of mass 1500 kg moving at 10 m/s is brought to rest in 2 s. Find the average braking force.
items.markingKey: a = (0 − 10)/2 = −5 m/s²; F = ma = 1500 × 5 = 7500 N, opposite to the motion. (or F = change in momentum ÷ time = 15000/2)

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.15 kg moving at 20 m/s is hit back by a bat with a speed of 20 m/s in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.01 s. Find the change in momentum and the average force.
items.answer: Change in momentum 6 kg m/s; force 600 N
items.markingKey: Taking the return direction as positive: Δp = m(v − (−u)) = 0.15 × (20 + 20) = 6 kg m/s; F = Δp/t = 6/0.01 = 600 N.

items.stem:
Read: In a crash test, a dummy of mass 60 kg moving at 10 m/s is stopped in 0.05 s when it hits the dashboard, but in 0.4 s when an airbag opens.
(i) Find the momentum of the dummy before the crash. (ii) Find the average force without the airbag. (iii) Find the average force with the airbag. (iv) Which law explains why the airbag reduces injury?
items.answer: (i) 600 kg m/s. (ii) 12000 N. (iii) 1500 N. (iv) Newton's second law (F = change in momentum ÷ time).
items.markingKey: 1 mark each part.

items.stem: A ball of mass 0.4 kg moving at 20 m/s is hit back by a bat with a speed of 25 m/s in the opposite direction. The contact lasts 0.01 s. Find the change in momentum and the average force.
items.answer: Change in momentum 18 kg m/s; force 1800 N
items.markingKey: Taking the return direction as positive: Δp = m(v − (−u)) = 0.4 × (25 + 20) = 18 kg m/s; F = Δp/t = 18/0.01 = 1800 N.

items.stem: A truck and a car are moving with the same momentum. If the same braking force acts on both, which stops first? Which travels farther before stopping?
items.answer: Same momentum and same force ⇒ same stopping time (t = p/F). Car has smaller mass, hence greater velocity, so it travels farther (s = p²/2mF is larger for the smaller mass).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: same time. 1 mark: car farther. 1 mark: reasoning.

items.stem: Why is it easier to stop a tennis ball than a cricket ball moving at the same speed?
items.answer: The cricket ball has more mass, so more momentum; more force or time is needed to stop it.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: more mass/momentum. 1 mark: more force needed.

items.stem: What force is needed to give a mass of 500 kg an acceleration of 2 m/s²?
Define the law of conservation of momentum.
items.answer: The law that the total momentum of a system of objects remains constant if no external unbalanced force acts on it
items.markingKey: 1 mark: The law of conservation of momentum – the law that the total momentum of a system of objects remains constant if no external unbalanced force acts on it.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 20 g is fired from a gun of mass 3 kg with a velocity of 300 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
items.markingKey: (a) Initial momentum = 0. 0.02 × 300 + 3 × V = 0 ⇒ V = −2 m/s (opposite to the bullet).

items.stem: If action and reaction are equal and opposite, why do they not cancel each other?
items.answer: They act on two different objects, so each produces its own effect.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: different objects. 1 mark: no cancellation.

items.stem: A bullet of mass 20 g is fired from a gun of mass 4 kg with a velocity of 400 m/s. Find the recoil velocity of the gun.
items.markingKey: Initial momentum = 0. 0.02 × 400 + 4 × V = 0 ⇒ V = −2 m/s (opposite to the bullet).

items.stem: A trolley of mass 4 kg moving at 4 m/s collides with a stationary trolley of mass 1 kg, and they move together. Find their common velocity.

Ball A (0.1 kg) moving at 5 m/s hits ball B (0.2 kg) moving at 1 m/s along the same line. After the collision A moves at 1 m/s in its original direction (negative means reversed). Find the velocity of B.
items.markingKey: m₁u₁ + m₂u₂ = m₁v₁ + m₂v₂ ⇒ 0.1×5 + 0.2×1 = 0.1×1 + 0.2v₂ ⇒ v₂ = 3 m/s.

items.stem: An astronaut floating in space throws a 2 kg tool at 3 m/s away from the spacecraft. If her mass with suit is 100 kg, what happens to her and why?
items.answer: She moves in the opposite direction at 2 × 3 ÷ 100 = 0.06 m/s, because total momentum must stay zero (no external force).
items.markingKey: 1 mark: direction. 1 mark: 0.06 m/s. 1 mark: conservation.

items.stem: Two identical trolleys are tied together with a compressed spring between them and are at rest. The string is cut. Predict their motion and explain.
items.answer: They move apart in opposite directions with equal speeds: the spring pushes both equally (third law) and the total momentum stays zero.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: opposite directions. 1 mark: equal speeds. 1 mark: reasoning.

items.stem: What is meant by friction?
items.answer: The force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact
items.markingKey: 1 mark: Friction – the force that opposes the relative motion between two surfaces in contact.

items.stem: A box of mass 10 kg is pushed along a floor with a force of 80 N. The friction force is 30 N. Find the acceleration of the box.
Why does a car need a continuous push from its engine to move at constant velocity on a level road?
items.answer: Friction and air resistance oppose the motion; the engine force balances them, so the net force is zero and velocity stays constant.
items.markingKey: 1 mark: opposing forces. 1 mark: balanced, constant velocity.
